summary: OSPF Router LSAs always include advertised links in the default SPF computation, which is a problem for non-default computations such as Flexible Algorithms (RFC 9350). This Standards Track document uses the metric LSLinkInfinity to advertise links that the base SPF should not use. It updates RFC 5443, RFC 6987, RFC 8379, and RFC 8770.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF puts every link it advertises into the ordinary route calculation, even a link that is only meant for a special purpose such as traffic engineering. This RFC gives the metric 0xffff a second meaning, so that a router can say a link exists but must not be used, and adds a capability bit that keeps old and new routers from disagreeing about it.

questions: how to advertise unreachable links in ospf
subtitle: How OSPF can advertise a link that the normal route calculation must ignore, using the metric 0xffff.

tldr.problem: OSPF router link state advertisements always include every advertised link in the default shortest path calculation, so a link meant only for traffic engineering or for a Flexible Algorithm still attracts ordinary traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The document gives the metric value 0xffff, LSLinkInfinity, a new meaning: a link advertised with it is left out of the path computation. Because that changes an existing meaning, routers may only act on it once every router in the area has advertised an Unreachable Link capability bit in a Router Information LSA.
tldr.outcome: Links can be advertised for a non-default computation and excluded from the default one. It also updates RFC 5443, RFC 6987, RFC 8379 and RFC 8770 so that they use the new value 0xfffe for links that stay reachable but are discouraged for transit traffic.

facts.label: Capability advertisement
facts.value: Area-scoped Router Information LSA with a Router Functional Capabilities TLV

facts.label: Auto-costing limit
facts.value: The maximum computed cost is limited to 0xfffe

today: RFC 10041 is a Proposed Standard from September 2026. It updates RFC 5443, RFC 6987, RFC 8379 and RFC 8770 so that they advertise 0xfffe rather than 0xffff, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with the Link Metric
sections.content:
OSPF Router Link State Advertisements use fixed-format encodings that always include advertised links in the default shortest path calculation. A link may be required for Traffic Engineering paths but not intended for hop-by-hop routing, or it may be used exclusively by a Flexible Algorithm, as described in RFC 9350, while being excluded from the default algorithm.

To advertise such links as unreachable, the metric LSLinkInfinity (0xffff) is used, and routers that support this specification exclude the link from the shortest path calculation, subject to the backward compatibility rules in Section 3.2.

The same value is already in use for other purposes, which is why the document also introduces MaxReachableLinkMetric (0xfffe). The Stub Router Advertisement specification, RFC 6987, defines MaxLinkMetric (0xffff) to indicate that a router LSA link should only be used for transit IP traffic as a last resort. When a router supports the Unreachable Link capability, its stub router links are advertised as 0xfffe instead. The LDP IGP Synchronization specification, RFC 5443, specifies advertising 0xffff to say that although the OSPF adjacency is in FULL state, LDP has not synchronized between the neighbours and transit traffic is discouraged; that too becomes 0xfffe. And OSPF Graceful Link Shutdown, RFC 8379, specifies advertising 0xffff to say that the link is about to be taken out of service and transit traffic is discouraged, which again becomes 0xfffe.
sections.plainLanguage: The value 0xffff already means something in OSPF: a link that is reachable but discouraged for through traffic. This RFC gives that same number a new meaning for one specific case, and moves the old meaning to the next value down, 0xfffe.

sections.title: Two Use Cases
sections.content:
The first case is Traffic Engineering. In the topology in the RFC, the link between nodes A and E is only to be used for Traffic Engineering. Because the link is advertised by default, it is included in the base shortest path calculation for the default topology, and it may be used for hop-by-hop routing there.

The second case is a Flexible Algorithm. The links between nodes A and B and between C and D are to be used exclusively for a Flexible Algorithm devoted to specific traffic, and they carry an Extended Administrative Group attribute specifying the Red colour. Flex-Algorithm 128 is enabled on nodes A, B, C and D, with an EAG rule that includes Red, and the Metric-Type is designated to be a type other than the OSPF metric, so OSPF computes routes for Flex-Algorithm 128 using these links.

The problem is that the Red links are also included in the default algorithm calculation, because they are reachable. If the OSPF metrics for all the Red links are advertised as unreachable, they are excluded from the default shortest path calculation, and the Red links from A to B and from C to D can then be used exclusively by the Flex-Algorithm 128 calculation.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives two examples. A link kept for traffic engineering would otherwise pull ordinary traffic onto it, and a link reserved for one Flexible Algorithm would also be offered to the default algorithm. Advertising it as unreachable keeps it out of the default calculation.

sections.title: Advertising an Unreachable Link
sections.content:
The rule is that if the OSPF metric of a link is advertised as LSLinkInfinity (0xffff), it must not be considered during the associated shortest path computation. This applies both to the Flexible Algorithm computation of RFC 9350 and to the base shortest path, as long as LSLinkInfinity is specified for the OSPF metric.

While the interpretation of LSLinkInfinity is only required in the base topology, because interpretation in other topologies is optional under RFC 4915, routers that support this specification must interpret LSLinkInfinity as unreachable consistently during the associated computation. The interpretation also applies to Flexible Algorithm computations that use the OSPF link metric.

An OSPF metric of LSLinkInfinity meaning that a link is unreachable applies to the Router-LSA of RFC 2328 and RFC 5340, and to the Router-Link TLV of the OSPFv3 E-Router-LSA of RFC 8362.
sections.plainLanguage: A link advertised with the metric 0xffff is left out of the route calculation, both in the default topology and in the Flexible Algorithm computation that uses the OSPF metric. The rule covers both OSPFv2 router LSAs and the OSPFv3 router link TLV.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and the Capability Bit
sections.content:
Before this specification, OSPF treated links advertised with LSLinkInfinity as reachable, so a partial deployment can cause routing loops through inconsistent interpretation. In the example in the RFC, link D-F is advertised with LSLinkInfinity. Router B supports the new meaning and router A does not. A considers D-F reachable, so its shortest path to F is A, B, D, F, and it forwards the packet to B. B considers D-F unreachable, so its shortest path to F is B, A, C, E, F, and it sends the packet back to A. The result is a loop.

To avoid that, routers that support the new meaning advertise an area-scoped Router Information LSA with a Router Functional Capabilities TLV, as defined in RFC 7770, that includes a Router Functional Capability bit numbered 0 and named Unreachable Link. The value of the bit is under configuration.

The rule is that routers must not treat links with an advertised metric of LSLinkInfinity as unreachable unless all routers in the area, meaning all routers with router LSAs in the area link state database, have advertised this capability in an OSPFv2 Router Information Opaque LSA or an OSPFv3 Router Information LSA. When every router in the area has advertised it, such links must be treated as unreachable. When the number of routers in the area that do not support the capability changes to zero, or from zero to more than zero, all routers in the area must recalculate their routes.

The RFC also describes what happens while the capability is propagating. If a new router that does not support the capability joins an area, it takes some time for its Router Information LSA to reach every router. During that time the routers in the area gradually notice the router that lacks the capability and revert to treating links with the maximum metric as reachable, and that inconsistency can cause transient routing loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Because 0xffff used to mean something else, routers may only act on the new meaning when every router in the area has said it understands it. Each router says so with a capability bit in a Router Information LSA. Until every router has said so, the old meaning applies.

sections.title: Updating the Other Specifications
sections.content:
Three specifications that use 0xffff to mean a link that stays reachable but is discouraged for transit traffic are changed to use 0xfffe instead, because the value 0xffff now has the stronger unreachable meaning.

For the Stub Router Advertisement of RFC 6987, the stub router maximum metric must be updated to MaxReachableLinkMetric (0xfffe), and a router that supports both the stub router advertisement and the Unreachable Link capability must be able to advertise all of its non-stub links with a link cost of 0xfffe. The RFC explains why this is safe: MaxLinkMetric only indicates an unreachable link when every router in the area supports this specification, and in that case every router in the area also supports the use of 0xfffe for the stub router links. If any router in the area lacks the capability, all routers treat links advertised with 0xffff as reachable, as Section 3.2 requires. This document updates RFC 6987 and RFC 8770.

For LDP IGP Synchronization in RFC 5443, the use of 0xffff to discourage the use of a link until LDP is fully operational must be updated to 0xfffe. The link is kept in the topology so that IP traffic can still use it as a last resort, for example when LDP packets between OSPF router loopback addresses are lost or when there is a network failure.

For OSPF Graceful Link Shutdown in RFC 8379, the use of 0xffff to discourage the use of a link before it is taken out of service must be updated to 0xfffe, again so that the link stays in the topology and can be used as a last resort before a planned shutdown.
sections.plainLanguage: Three other specifications used 0xffff to mean that a link stays reachable but should not carry through traffic. They now use 0xfffe, so that 0xffff can be reserved for the new meaning. In each case the link stays in the topology and can still be used if there is no alternative.

sections.title: Configuration and the YANG Model
sections.content:
Support of the Unreachable Link capability must be configurable, and the default must be to not advertise the capability, so the functional capability in the area-scoped OSPF Router Information LSA is false by default.

Some networks still want links with the maximum metric to be treated as reachable. The RFC gives the example of a network where the cost of a link is computed automatically from the inverse of its bandwidth, and a mix of low-speed and high-speed links can make that computation produce the maximum metric. Implementations that support this document and use auto-costing must therefore limit the maximum computed cost to MaxReachableLinkMetric (0xfffe).

Three YANG modules are defined. The iana-ospf-functional-cap-bits module holds the identities for the OSPF Router Functional Capabilities in the IANA registry, and is updated as that registry changes. The ietf-ospf-functional-capability and ietf-ospf-unreachable-links modules configure and manage the use of LSLinkInfinity for unreachable links, and augment the OSPF YANG data model of RFC 9129 and the routing management model of RFC 8349.

The first of the two operational modules augments the Router Capabilities TLV in the OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 Router Information structures, at area, link and autonomous system scope, with a read-only list of functional capabilities. The second augments the OSPF area with a read-write container for unreachable link advertisement, holding a read-write boolean enabled, and augments the OSPF interface with a read-write boolean advertise-unreachable-link.
sections.plainLanguage: The capability is off by default, so a network only changes behaviour when an operator turns it on. The RFC also adds YANG modules so that management software can read the capability and switch the per-area and per-interface settings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A compromised OSPF router could advertise changes to its Unreachable Link capability rapidly, which would cause repeated route recalculations on the routers in the area that support this specification. Routers that support this specification are therefore recommended to support the shortest path back-off delay algorithm of RFC 8405. The security considerations of RFC 2328, RFC 5340, RFC 6987 and RFC 7770 also apply to this extension.

The two YANG modules define data models meant to be reached over a management protocol such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. Such protocols have to use a secure transport layer, such as SSH, TLS or QUIC, and they have to use mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model of RFC 8341 provides the means to restrict particular users to a pre-configured subset of operations and content.

The RFC lists the writable data nodes, which are the enabled boolean under the area's unreachable link advertisement container and the advertise-unreachable-link boolean under an interface. Write or delete operations on them without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations, because an unprotected change can prevent the LSLinkInfinity metric from being interpreted as unreachable, or cause a link to be advertised as unreachable. The RFC also notes that the readable data nodes may be sensitive, because exposing the unreachable link configuration can be useful in mounting a denial-of-service attack.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that lies about its capability could make the whole area recalculate its routes repeatedly, so the RFC recommends the standard back-off delay for route computation. Management access to the new settings must be protected, because a change to them can alter how the whole area routes traffic.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document defines a new bit in the OSPF Router Functional Capability Bits registry: bit number 0, with the capability name Unreachable Link.

Three new URIs are registered in the ns registry of the IETF XML Registry, for the XML namespaces of the modules iana-ospf-functional-cap-bits, ietf-ospf-functional-capability and ietf-ospf-unreachable-links. Three new module names are registered in the YANG Module Names registry: iana-ospf-functional-cap-bits, which is maintained by IANA, and ietf-ospf-functional-capability and ietf-ospf-unreachable-links, which are not.

The IANA-maintained module mirrors the OSPF Router Functional Capability Bits registry and carries a note that new values must not be added to the module directly, but to the registry instead. When a value is added to the registry, a new identity statement is added to the module, named after the registry entry in lowercase with spaces replaced by hyphens, and carrying a base of functional-capability, the unabbreviated capability name as its description and the registry references.
sections.plainLanguage: The capability gets a number in IANA's registry of OSPF router capabilities, and the three YANG modules are registered with their own names and namespaces so that management software can find them.

viz.caption: The two cases the RFC describes

items.title: Traffic Engineering
items.text: A link kept only for traffic engineering paths is advertised by default, so it is included in the base shortest path calculation and may carry hop-by-hop traffic.

items.title: Flexible Algorithm
items.text: Links reserved for Flex-Algorithm 128, marked with the Red Extended Administrative Group, are also used by the default algorithm because they are reachable.

items.title: The fix
items.text: Advertising their OSPF metrics as unreachable removes them from the default calculation, so they are used only by the computation that wants them.
